533.title: V'Zot HaBerachah: an inheritance (Deuteronomy 33:4)
533.hook: the Torah is "the inheritance of the congregation of Jacob", learned from childhood
533.howItsDone: Following the Talmud, the verse 'Torah tzivah lanu Moshe' is traditionally among the first a young child learns, often sung, together with the first line of the Shema.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses' last words: blessings, tribe by tribe. Your line was end with a blessing. Who did you bless? Today, one verse from among those blessings, and it's the one the Talmud says a child learns first. Day five hundred thirty-three.

What's the first sentence you remember learning by heart? A nursery rhyme, a prayer at bedtime, a pledge at school, a line from a song. Whatever it was, it may still be in there, word for word. The Talmud says that when a Jewish child first begins to talk, there's a particular verse a parent should teach. It isn't from Genesis, at the beginning of everything. It's from the very end of the Torah, tucked in among Moses' blessings.
screen: `A RHYME, A PLEDGE, A SONG.` → `STILL THERE, WORD FOR WORD.` → `A CHILD'S FIRST VERSE.`

segments.voice: "Moses commanded us a law, An inheritance of the congregation of Jacob." In Hebrew: Torah tzivah lanu Moshe, morashah kehillat Ya'akov. The Talmud, in Sukkah, says that as soon as a child can speak, the father teaches him this verse, along with the first line of the Shema. Notice the little word lanu, to us. A child's first verse already says we. Now the second half. Morashah, inheritance. And whose inheritance is it? Not the priests'. Not the scholars'. The congregation of Jacob: everyone. Maimonides makes the point sharply. Israel was given three crowns, he writes. The crown of priesthood went to Aaron's family. The crown of kingship went to David's line. But the crown of Torah is set out for anyone who wants it: whoever wishes may come and take it. The Talmud also plays with the word. It reads morashah, inheritance, as if it said me'orasah, betrothed: the Torah isn't only handed down like property; it's meant to be loved. And some teachers notice that Hebrew has two words for inheritance. Yerushah is what you receive. Morashah, they suggest, is a heritage you hold in order to pass it on. Either way, the first verse a child learns says: this belongs to you, and to all of us.
screen: `TORAH TZIVAH LANU MOSHE.` · `A CHILD'S FIRST VERSE.` · `THREE CROWNS, ONE OPEN TO ALL.` · `INHERITED, AND HANDED ON.` · then, large: `INHERITANCE FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one line by heart. Settle, and breathe. Choose a short line: this verse, if you like, Moses commanded us a law, an inheritance of the congregation of Jacob. Or any line from these weeks that has stayed with you. Say it once. Close your eyes, and say it again without looking. Then again. Notice which word slips, and go back for it. By the bell, it can be yours. The bell holds the time.
V'Zot HaBerachah. And this is the blessing. And in it, morashah: an inheritance for the whole congregation.
Your line: inheritance for everyone. Today, say your learned line once more, and teach it, or any line you love, to one other person. Day five hundred thirty-three.

534.title: V'Zot HaBerachah: from the mountain (Deuteronomy 34:1–4)
534.hook: from Mount Nebo Moses sees the land he won't enter
534.tomorrow: V'Zot HaBerachah: no one knows his grave (Deuteronomy 34:5–6)
534.howItsDone: The final chapter of Deuteronomy, with Moses on Mount Nebo, is read on Simchat Torah; in many communities its closing verses are read with special honor as the end of the yearly Torah cycle.

segments.voice: Yesterday, morashah, the inheritance of everyone. Your line was inheritance for everyone. Did your learned line stay with you? Today, Moses climbs one last mountain. Day five hundred thirty-four.

Most people carry at least one goal they may not live to see finished. A child fully grown. A building completed. A cause won. A garden that will only be beautiful in thirty years. Grandparents plant trees their grandchildren will sit under. Founders start things they'll have to hand on. It's one of the strangest human habits: working hard toward a place you may never stand in. Moses spent forty years walking toward a land. Today he gets to see it.
screen: `A TREE FOR THE GRANDCHILDREN.` → `A PLACE YOU MAY NEVER STAND.` → `FORTY YEARS, AND A VIEW.`

segments.voice: Moses goes up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, across from Jericho. And God shows him the land: Gilead as far as Dan, the lands of the tribes, the hill country, the plain, all the way to the western sea, and the Negev in the south. Then God says: "This is the land which I swore unto Abraham, unto Isaac, and unto Jacob, saying: I will give it unto thy seed; I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither." He sees all of it. He will not enter. Earlier, in Va'etchanan, Moses had pleaded to be allowed across. A midrash counts his pleading as five hundred fifteen prayers, the number value of the Hebrew word va'etchanan, and I pleaded. The answer was still no. And yet here he climbs anyway. The text records no complaint at the top. Only seeing. Some commentators read the view as a gift. Rashi says God showed Moses not just the land but its future, what would happen there to his people for generations. Others read it simply. He saw the place he'd led everyone toward, and the text lets that be enough. A mountain traditionally identified as Nebo still stands in Jordan today, looking west. The Torah doesn't hide the cost. He doesn't arrive. But he's allowed to see.
screen: `UP TO NEBO, TO THE TOP OF PISGAH.` · `FROM DAN TO THE WESTERN SEA.` · `THOU SHALT NOT GO OVER.` · `SEEING IS ALLOWED.` · then, large: `SEE IT FROM THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a goal you may not reach. Settle, and breathe. Name one thing you're working toward that might take longer than your life, or might never fully happen. A family healed. A town changed. A child's future. A world a little fairer. Picture yourself on a hilltop, looking at it from a distance. You don't have to be standing in it to care about it. Let yourself see it clearly, and let the seeing be enough for now. The bell holds the time.
V'Zot HaBerachah. And this is the blessing. And in it, the view from Nebo: the land Moses sees, and won't enter.
Your line: see it from the mountain. Today, do one small thing for a goal you may never see finished. Day five hundred thirty-four.

535.title: V'Zot HaBerachah: no one knows his grave (Deuteronomy 34:5–6)
535.hook: God buries Moses, and no one knows his grave to this day
535.howItsDone: Jewish tradition calls caring for the dead chesed shel emet, a true kindness, since it can't be repaid; local chevra kadisha societies prepare bodies for burial, and tradition places Moses' death on the 7th of Adar, a day some burial societies mark.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the view from Nebo. Your line was see it from the mountain. What goal did you look at? Today, the death of Moses, and a strange detail about his grave. Day five hundred thirty-five.

Pyramids. Mausoleums. A marble tomb with a line of visitors outside. Famous people are often given famous graves, and pilgrims travel far to stand where a founder lies. They leave flowers, candles, notes, stones. Some tombs become places of prayer. Moses, the teacher at the center of the Torah, dies on a mountain in Moab. And the text goes out of its way to tell us there is nothing to visit.
screen: `PYRAMIDS AND MAUSOLEUMS.` → `PILGRIMS AT THE TOMB.` → `NOTHING TO VISIT.`

segments.voice: So Moses, the servant of God, dies there in the land of Moab, at God's word. He is buried in a valley opposite Beth-peor, the text says, "and no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day." Who buried him? The Hebrew simply says: he buried him. Rashi says it was God, in His glory. The Talmud, in Sotah, takes that seriously and turns it into a teaching about how people should live. God clothed Adam and Eve. God visited Abraham when he was healing. God comforted Isaac when he mourned. And God buried Moses. So, the Talmud says, walk in God's ways: clothe, visit, comfort, bury. When volunteers of a chevra kadisha, a Jewish burial society, care for the body of someone who has died, they're walking in that line. And the hidden grave? The text doesn't say why. One explanation often given is that the people would have made it a place of worship, and Moses had always pointed beyond himself. Whatever the reason, the effect is clear. No shrine. No relic. What remains of Moses is what he taught. And the teaching isn't left in one place. It's in each Torah scroll, read aloud week by week. Moses' grave is unknown. His words are read wherever the scroll is opened.
screen: `MOSES DIES IN THE LAND OF MOAB.` · `WHO BURIED HIM?` · `CLOTHE, VISIT, COMFORT, BURY.` · `NO SHRINE, ONLY TEACHING.` · then, large: `NO GRAVE, ONLY TEACHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let a legacy be the teaching. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who has died whose words or habits still live in you. A grandmother's saying, a teacher's correction, a friend's way of laughing at trouble. You don't need a grave to find them. Where do they show up in your own life? Name one thing they taught you. Then think of one thing you'd like to pass on in the same way, so that it outlasts you. The bell holds the time.
V'Zot HaBerachah. And this is the blessing. A portion that ends with a death, an unknown grave, and a teaching that stays.
Your line: no grave, only teaching. Today, pass on one thing someone taught you, and say their name when you do. Day five hundred thirty-five.

screen: `DAY 535 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: V'ZOT HABERACHAH: FACE TO FACE (DEUTERONOMY 34:10–12).`

536.title: V'Zot HaBerachah: face to face (Deuteronomy 34:10–12)
536.hook: no prophet arose like Moses, "whom the LORD knew face to face"
536.howItsDone: In Jewish speech Moses is commonly called Moshe Rabbenu, 'Moses our teacher', and the closing verses of Deuteronomy are read on Simchat Torah as the yearly Torah cycle ends.

segments.voice: Yesterday in V'Zot HaBerachah, the grave no one knows. Your line was no grave, only teaching. What did you pass on, and in whose name? Today, the Torah's last word about Moses himself. Day five hundred thirty-six.

A teacher stays after class to explain it one more time. A coach sees something in a kid before the kid does. A grandparent explains the world over breakfast. People like this rarely ask for credit, and often never hear what they did. Their names fade, while what they taught keeps going. The Torah's final verses are, in a way, a tribute to a teacher. They say who Moses was, now that he's gone.
screen: `A TEACHER AFTER CLASS.` → `A GRANDPARENT AT BREAKFAST.` → `A TRIBUTE AT THE END.`

segments.voice: "And there hath not arisen a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face." Then the verses recall the signs in Egypt and the mighty hand, done in the sight of all Israel. Face to face: in Hebrew, panim el panim. Earlier, in Numbers, God explains the difference to Moses' own brother and sister: with other prophets I speak in visions and dreams, but with Moses, mouth to mouth. The text presents that closeness as direct, unlike any other. Maimonides made that uniqueness one of his thirteen principles of faith: that Moses' prophecy stands above that of every other prophet. And yet, notice the title Jewish tradition actually gives him. Not Moses our prophet. Not Moses our king. Moshe Rabbenu: Moses our teacher. He led slaves out of Egypt, stood at the sea, met God on a mountain, and the name that stuck is teacher. There's a quiet second meaning in face to face. It describes something no one else had: God and Moses. But a teacher is known face to face too, by the students sitting across the table. In the tradition, Moses' closeness to God reaches later generations through what he taught. The book closes, and the tribute it chooses is this: he was known, close up. And through him, so were the words.
screen: `NO PROPHET SINCE LIKE MOSES.` · `PANIM EL PANIM.` · `MAIMONIDES' SEVENTH PRINCIPLE.` · `MOSHE RABBENU: MOSES OUR TEACHER.` · then, large: `FACE TO FACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a teacher who shaped you. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a teacher of any kind. A schoolteacher, a rabbi, a boss, a parent, an older friend. See their face, close up. What did they give you that you still use? Thank them in your mind. Then ask yourself whether you could tell them for real. A message, a letter, a call. If they've died, tell someone else about them, by name. The bell holds the time.
V'Zot HaBerachah. And this is the blessing. Ending with Moses, known face to face, and remembered as our teacher.
Your line: face to face. Today, thank a teacher who shaped you, directly if you can, or tell someone about them. Day five hundred thirty-six.

screen: `DAY 536 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SIMCHAT TORAH CLOSE: THE CIRCLE.`

537.title: Simchat Torah close: the circle
537.hook: the Torah's last letter and first letter spell lev, heart; the scroll rolls straight on
537.howItsDone: On Simchat Torah, congregations dance with the Torah scrolls in seven circuits (hakafot), read the end of Deuteronomy, and immediately begin Genesis again; the two readers are honored as chatan Torah and chatan Bereshit, and some communities honor women with parallel titles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses, known face to face, and remembered as our teacher. Your line was face to face. Who did you thank? Today, the Torah's very last word, and what happens right after it. Day five hundred thirty-seven.

On Simchat Torah, synagogues get loud. The scrolls come out of the ark and people dance with them, around and around the room, seven circuits, sometimes spilling out into the street. Children wave flags. Someone who hasn't set foot inside all year is handed a scroll to hold. And in the middle of all that, something quiet and precise happens at the reading table. The last words of the Torah are read aloud. And then, without stopping, the first.
screen: `SCROLLS OUT OF THE ARK.` → `SEVEN CIRCUITS OF DANCING.` → `THE LAST WORDS, THEN THE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Deuteronomy ends with the words in the sight of all Israel; in Hebrew, le'einei kol Yisrael. So the last letter of the whole Torah is the lamed at the end of Yisrael. Genesis begins with bereshit, in the beginning, and its first letter is bet. Put the last letter and the first together, lamed and bet, and they spell lev: heart. Some teachers point this out. The Torah, end joined to beginning, makes a heart. On Simchat Torah, the person honored with reading the end is called the chatan Torah, the bridegroom of the Torah. The one honored with starting again is the chatan Bereshit, the bridegroom of the beginning. The scroll isn't rolled up and put away for a rest. It's rolled straight back to its start, and the same day the reading begins again: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." Since day three hundred thirty-two, this path has walked from the plagues in Egypt through the rest of Exodus, through Leviticus and Numbers, and these last weeks through Deuteronomy, Moses' farewell. The forgotten sheaf and the first fruits. Choose life. Write your own. The song, the blessing, the grave no one knows, face to face. Tomorrow a new part of the year begins: the siddur, the prayer book, walked page by page. But the Torah doesn't stop. The end touches the beginning.
screen: `LE'EINEI KOL YISRAEL.` · `LAMED AND BET SPELL LEV.` · `TWO BRIDEGROOMS OF THE TORAH.` · `ROLLED STRAIGHT BACK TO THE START.` · then, large: `THE END TOUCHES THE BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the last and first verses together. Settle, and breathe. Here is the end of the Torah: Moses' mighty deeds, done in the sight of all Israel. And here is the beginning: in the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. Say them one after the other, slowly, with no pause in between. Notice what it's like to finish and start in the same breath. Then think of something in your own life that's ending. Where might it touch a beginning? The bell holds the time.
Simchat Torah. Rejoicing in the Torah. The day the last verse is read and the first begins again, with no gap between.
Your line: the end touches the beginning. Today, when you finish something, start the next small thing right away, without the gap. Day five hundred thirty-seven.

538.title: The siddur
538.hook: the prayer book, named "order", the most-used Jewish book after the Torah
538.howItsDone: Jews who pray daily use a siddur for the morning, afternoon and evening services, and a related book, the machzor, for the High Holy Days. Different communities follow different rites (nusach), such as Ashkenaz, Sefard and Edot HaMizrach.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the circle: the Torah's last letter and its first, together spelling heart. Your line was the end touches the beginning. What did you finish, and start? Today, a new book. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

Near the door of a synagogue there's often a shelf of matching books, worn soft at the corners. One page carries a wine stain from a holiday, another a child's pencil mark, another the crease of a hand that held it for a lifetime. People take one on the way in without thinking. It isn't the Torah scroll. For a Jew who prays every day, it may be the book held more often than any other. For the next stretch of this year, we'll walk through it, in order.
screen: `A SHELF BY THE DOOR.` → `WORN SOFT AT THE CORNERS.` → `THE BOOK HELD MOST OFTEN.`

segments.voice: The word is siddur. It comes from seder, order, the same root as the Passover seder, the ordered meal. A siddur is the prayer book: the weekday prayers, the Sabbath and festival prayers, blessings for food and for waking up, all arranged in the order they're said. That order is the point. Jewish prayer isn't mostly a blank page. It has a shape: blessings, then psalms, then the Shema, then the standing prayer, then the closing. The Talmud discusses many of these prayers long before anyone bound them into one volume. Among the oldest written orders of prayer that survive are two from the geonim, the heads of the academies in Babylonia: the order of Rav Amram Gaon, and the siddur of Rav Saadia Gaon. Since then, many versions have grown. Ashkenazi Jews, from Central and Eastern Europe, have their rite. Sephardi and Mizrahi Jews, from Spain, North Africa and the Middle East, have theirs. Yemenite communities, Hasidic communities and the modern movements each have siddurim of their own. The core is shared; the details differ, and each community keeps its own. Why give prayer an order at all? One answer: on the days you have no words, the siddur has them. On the days you have too many, it gives them a path. Starting tomorrow, we'll open it, step by step.
screen: `SIDDUR, FROM SEDER: ORDER.` · `PRAYER WITH A SHAPE.` · `AMRAM GAON AND SAADIA GAON.` · `MANY RITES, ONE CORE.` · then, large: `PRAYER HAS AN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold or open a siddur. If you have one, take it off the shelf and simply hold it. Feel its weight. Open it anywhere and read one line, in Hebrew or in translation. If you don't have one, hold any book you've gone back to many times, and notice why you keep returning. Then remember that people have prayed these words, in this order, from books like this, across many generations. The bell holds the time.
Siddur. Order. The Jewish prayer book: the daily prayers, arranged in the order they're said.
Your line: prayer has an order. Today, notice the order of one part of your day, your morning or your evening, and see what shape it already has. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

539.title: Three times a day (Berakhot 26b)
539.hook: morning, afternoon and evening prayer are linked to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, or to the Temple offerings
539.howItsDone: Observant Jews pray three services daily: shacharit in the morning, minchah in the afternoon and ma'ariv (also called arvit) in the evening, often with a minyan, a quorum of ten, in synagogue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the siddur, the book of order. Your line was prayer has an order. What shape did your day already have? Today, the first order inside it: when. Day five hundred thirty-nine.

Most people already live by a rhythm of three. Breakfast, lunch, dinner. Waking up, the afternoon slump, winding down at night. Three times a day, the mood of the day tips over into something new. Jewish prayer is built on the same three hinges: shacharit in the morning, minchah in the afternoon, ma'ariv in the evening. The Talmud asks a simple question about them. Where did these three times come from? It gives two answers, and keeps both.
screen: `BREAKFAST, LUNCH, DINNER.` → `SHACHARIT, MINCHAH, MA'ARIV.` → `TWO ANSWERS, BOTH KEPT.`

segments.voice: In Berakhot, on page twenty-six, Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Hanina says: the prayers were established by the patriarchs. Abraham set the morning prayer: the Torah says he rose early in the morning and went to the place where he had stood before God. Isaac set the afternoon prayer: "And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide." Jacob set the evening prayer: night was falling when he came upon a certain place, and the Talmud reads that word, vayifga, as meeting God in prayer. Rabbi Yehoshua son of Levi says something else: the prayers were set to match the daily offerings in the Temple, morning and afternoon, with the evening prayer matching the parts that burned on the altar through the night. The Talmud doesn't throw either answer away. It weaves them together: the patriarchs began these prayers, and the rabbis tied them to the offerings. Two ways of seeing the same three times. One says prayer is personal, like a man walking alone in a field at dusk. The other says prayer is shared and regular, like the Temple's daily service. The Talmud keeps both pictures on the same page. And that closes a week that crossed a border. It began in the last chapters of the Torah, with Moses seeing the land from the mountain and buried where no one knows, and it ends inside the prayer book: first its order, and now its three times a day.
screen: `ABRAHAM: THE MORNING.` · `ISAAC: IN THE FIELD AT EVENTIDE.` · `JACOB: MEETING THE PLACE AT NIGHT.` · `OR: THE TEMPLE'S DAILY OFFERINGS.` · then, large: `MORNING, AFTERNOON, EVENING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pause three times today. Settle, and breathe. Decide now on three moments: one in the morning, or right now, one in the afternoon, one at night. Tie each to something you already do: the first coffee, a late-afternoon break, brushing your teeth. At each one, stop for three breaths. If you pray, it could be a prayer you know. If not, the pause alone is enough. Picture all three now, like hinges in your day. The bell holds the time.
Three times a day. Shacharit, minchah, ma'ariv: morning, afternoon and evening, the three hinges of Jewish prayer.
Your line: morning, afternoon, evening. Today, take your three pauses at the three hinges of the day. Day five hundred thirty-nine.

fork.setup: two rabbis disagree: the three prayers come from the patriarchs, or from the Temple's daily offerings. what does the Talmud do?
fork.reveal: Berakhot 26b: the patriarchs established them, and the rabbis linked them to the offerings. personal and shared at once.

original.note: Hebrew: the morning, afternoon and evening prayers.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rule about how often to pray.
what it means: three hinges of the day, each tied to a patriarch or to the Temple's daily service.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 26b brings both opinions and harmonizes them; Jacob's vayifga (Genesis 28:11) is read as prayer.
